articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Oil Traders and Government Insiders in Latest Sanctions Round
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions on November 20, 2026, targeting Iranian oil traders and government-linked facilitators. These individuals and entities are accused of orchestrating schemes to sell Iranian oil abroad and illicitly funneling the revenues. This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' an initiative aimed at disrupting Iran's ability to generate revenue for its destabilizing activities.

The designations were imposed under two executive orders: one focusing on Iran's petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, and another utilizing counterterrorism authorities. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that the Iranian regime prioritizes its own interests over its citizens, even amidst domestic shortages of essential goods.

Among those designated are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, brother of the head of the Iranian Football Federation, who are alleged to lead a network selling oil from Iran's reserves. Other individuals sanctioned include Mohammadhossein Servati, son of IRGC Brig. Gen. Mohsen Servati, and Mojtaba Arabnejad, son of Mahan Air CEO Hamid Arabnejad, for their roles in supporting illicit oil sales and procurement for Mahan Air, an airline previously identified for transporting weapons and fighters for the IRGC-Quds Force.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Frequently Asked Questions Regarding Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) released new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning Cuba sanctions on November 20, 2026. This update aims to provide further clarity and guidance on existing regulations related to transactions involving Cuba. The issuance of these FAQs follows a period of intensified U.S. pressure on the Cuban economy.

These FAQs are intended to assist individuals and entities in understanding their compliance obligations under the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR) and other relevant executive orders. The U.S. has consistently maintained a comprehensive system of sanctions against Cuba for decades, with recent measures expanding the scope of targeted economic sectors.

The updated guidance comes amidst ongoing international debate regarding the impact of U.S. sanctions on the Cuban populace and the country's humanitarian situation. The United Nations General Assembly has repeatedly called for an end to the U.S. embargo against Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Illicit Drugs General License and New Counter Narcotics Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter narcotics designations and the issuance of Illicit Drugs General License 1 on November 19, 2026. General License 1 authorizes the wind down of transactions involving certain persons blocked on this date, providing a limited period for affected parties to cease their dealings.

These actions are part of ongoing efforts to combat international drug trafficking networks and their facilitators. The designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trade, aiming to disrupt their financial and operational capabilities.

In addition to the illicit drugs-related measures, OFAC also issued an amended Russia-related General License 131L, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH, along with two associated, amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs 1224 and 1225).

articles.headline: Treasury Targets Cyber Scam Operators and Armed Group Facilitators in Southeast Asia
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced cyber-related designations on November 19, 2026, targeting operators of cyber scams and facilitators of armed groups in Southeast Asia. This action underscores the U.S. commitment to disrupting malicious cyber activities and illicit financial flows globally.

These designations aim to expose and isolate individuals and entities that engage in cybercrime, including those involved in online fraud and other illicit digital activities. The Treasury Department highlighted the growing threat posed by such operations to the international financial system and national security.

The action also included updates to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, reflecting the addition of individuals and entities linked to these cyber-related illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt the financial networks and support structures of terrorist organizations worldwide.

The designations target individuals and entities found to be providing material support, financial services, or other forms of aid to terrorist groups. Such measures aim to isolate these actors from the international financial system and prevent them from funding their illicit activities.
The U.S. Treasury Department continues to utilize its authorities to counter global terrorism, working to safeguard the U.S. financial system from abuse by those who seek to finance acts of terror.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations with Terrorist Links
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter narcotics and counter terrorism designations on November 13, 2026, targeting several Guatemalan drug trafficking organizations. These groups are accused of supporting Mexican narco-terrorist cartels, highlighting the nexus between drug trafficking and terrorism.

Among the designated entities are 'Los Lorenzana,' also known as the Lorenzana Drug Trafficking Organization, identified as a transnational terrorist group. OFAC also imposed blocking sanctions against the 'Los Mendoza Drug Trafficking Organization' for supporting the Sinaloa Cartel.

Additionally, the counterterrorism authority was added to the existing narcotics designation for the 'Los Huistas Drug Trafficking Organization,' which is linked to both the Sinaloa Cartel and the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion (CJNG). These actions aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of these criminal organizations.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Listings
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an update to certain Iran designation listings on November 9, 2026. This administrative action clarifies and refines existing sanctions entries related to Iran, without necessarily introducing new designations.

The update includes the addition of a 'Secondary sanctions risk' warning to over 1,000 existing Iran sanctions entries, as well as to the Sectoral Sanctions Identifications (SSI) List entry for VTB Bank. This warning explicitly informs foreign banks of the potential consequences, such as restrictions on U.S. correspondent and payable-through accounts, if they knowingly facilitate significant transactions for blocked persons.

While no new individuals or entities were blocked as part of this specific update, the change enhances the visibility of secondary sanctions risks for compliance screeners and is expected to lead to faster payment rejections and increased de-risking of Iran-linked business by financial institutions and shippers.

articles.headline: U.S. Sanctions Cripple Financial Networks Sustaining the Iranian Regime
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026, targeting financial networks that sustain the Iranian regime. These actions are part of a broader strategy to intensify pressure on Iran and cut off its access to revenue used for destabilizing activities.

The sanctions aim to disrupt the flow of funds to the Iranian government and its proxies, including those involved in illicit oil sales and other revenue-generating schemes. This follows previous actions under 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which seeks to dismantle Iran's shadow fleet and other sanctions evasion tactics.

Earlier in November, the Treasury also announced sanctions targeting eight Canada-based money services businesses for their alleged involvement in transferring revenue from overseas oil sales to Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations designations on November 5, 2026. These actions target illicit networks that pose a threat to U.S. national security and the international financial system.

The designations aim to disrupt the activities of criminal groups involved in cybercrime, money laundering, and other illicit enterprises that often transcend national borders. By targeting these organizations, OFAC seeks to prevent them from accessing the U.S. financial system and leveraging their ill-gotten gains.
This action is part of a broader government effort to combat transnational crime and cyber threats, which often intersect and enable a wide range of illicit activities.

articles.headline: U.S. Expands Cuba Sanctions to Key Economic Sectors and Designates Entities
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination on November 5, 2026. This action significantly expands the scope of U.S. sanctions by making foreign firms operating in Cuba's electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors liable to sanctions.

The determination, signed by OFAC Director Bradley T. Smith, extends a provision of Executive Order 14404 of May 1, 2026, which authorizes sanctions on foreign persons found to operate in specific sectors of the Cuban economy. Concurrently, OFAC designated eight entities and two individuals, and identified five Cuban-flagged tankers as blocked property, linking them to Cuba's fuel shipping, state companies, and military supply.

Among the designated entities are Chinese military suppliers, including China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of China Electronics Technology Group Corporation, for materially assisting the Government of Cuba. This move has been condemned by both Cuban state media and China.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Fraudulent Ship Registries and Aviation Support for Iranian Regime
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, targeting fraudulent ship registries and entities providing aviation support to the Iranian regime. This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aimed at disrupting Iran's ability to evade sanctions through deceptive maritime practices.

OFAC also published an Iran-related OFAC Alert titled 'Iranian Shadow Fleet Reliance on False Flags for Sanctions Evasion.' This alert highlights the significant risk of designation or penalties for providing services to vessels that use false flags to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Iran.

The alert details how Iranian shadow fleet operators increasingly use fraudulent registries or falsely claim flags without proper registration to create a veneer of legitimacy. OFAC encourages service providers, including insurers and financial institutions, to conduct enhanced due diligence on vessels exhibiting such red flags to avoid engaging in sanctionable activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on November 4, 2026. This update provides further guidance and adjustments to existing sanctions policies concerning Venezuela. The specific details of the amended General License and FAQ were not immediately released but are intended to clarify permissible activities under the Venezuela sanctions program.

These amendments are part of OFAC's ongoing review and adjustment of sanctions programs to address evolving geopolitical and humanitarian considerations. The U.S. maintains a comprehensive sanctions regime against the Venezuelan government and its associated entities.

The issuance of updated guidance aims to assist stakeholders in navigating the complexities of the Venezuela sanctions, ensuring compliance while potentially facilitating certain transactions or activities as outlined in the amended license.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, reflecting ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions policy towards the country. The specific details of the changes were not immediately available.

General Licenses are issued by OFAC to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. Amendments to these licenses can expand, narrow, or clarify the scope of permissible activities.

This action is part of the U.S. government's dynamic approach to Iran sanctions, which often involves periodic updates and adjustments in response to various factors, including diplomatic efforts, regional developments, and humanitarian considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new North Korea designations on October 28, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter North Korea's illicit weapons programs and other destabilizing activities. The designations aim to disrupt financial networks and entities that support the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) regime.

The U.S. government continues to utilize sanctions to pressure North Korea to abandon its weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs. These measures typically target individuals, entities, and vessels involved in proliferation financing, cyber activities, and other illicit revenue generation for the DPRK.
International cooperation remains a key component of the strategy to enforce sanctions against North Korea and prevent its access to resources that could further its illicit programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Related to Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)-related designations on October 28, 2026. These actions are aimed at addressing ongoing instability, human rights abuses, and corruption within the region. The specific individuals or entities targeted were not immediately detailed.

U.S. sanctions programs related to the DRC typically target those who contribute to conflict, engage in serious human rights abuses, or participate in corrupt practices that undermine peace and stability in the country. These measures seek to promote accountability and encourage positive change.
The designations underscore the U.S. commitment to supporting good governance and human rights in the DRC, working with international partners to address the root causes of conflict and instability.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,529,685
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 27, 2026. The specific details of the violations were outlined in the enforcement release.

OFAC's enforcement actions serve to highlight the importance of robust sanctions compliance programs for companies operating internationally. Penalties are assessed based on various factors, including the nature of the violations, the company's cooperation, and any remedial measures taken.
This settlement underscores the continued vigilance of OFAC in enforcing U.S. sanctions laws across various industries and geographic locations.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle 475 apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 13, 2026. This settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action that also involved the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), which imposed significantly larger penalties for anti-money laundering failures.

The apparent violations by Bank of America spanned from September 2021 to April 2025 and involved transactions totaling approximately $14.8 million across various sanctions programs, including those related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. OFAC identified issues such as delayed updates to screening filters, analyst errors, and alert suppression rules, particularly concerning blocked banks in payment routing directories.

While the OFAC penalty is smaller compared to the AML fines, it highlights critical failures in the bank's sanctions screening program, including vendor data management, filter updates, alert prioritization, and human error. OFAC classified the violations as non-egregious and mostly not voluntarily disclosed.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015 Over Sanctioned Chinese Supplier
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations, as announced on October 9, 2026. The violations stemmed from arranging the shipment of a sugar packet-filling machine from a designated Chinese supplier.

The case involved Pegasus coordinating the purchase and shipment of a machine from Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., a Chinese supplier designated under Executive Order 14059 for its involvement in supplying equipment for counterfeit pill production. Youli had changed its name to Huizhou Youli Fushi Co., Ltd. after its designation, but its phone number and email address, both listed on the SDN List, remained unchanged.

OFAC found that Pegasus's screening process was insufficient, as it only screened the new name and failed to identify the sanctioned entity through other identifiers. Additionally, Pegasus initially provided an incomplete response to an OFAC administrative subpoena. The settlement reflects OFAC's determination that the violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, but also acknowledges Pegasus's remedial measures.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1,427,230
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 10, 2026. The specific details of the individual's violations were not immediately made public in the summary.

OFAC regularly pursues enforcement actions against individuals who violate U.S. sanctions laws, emphasizing that compliance obligations extend to all U.S. persons, regardless of their location. These penalties aim to deter illicit activities and uphold the integrity of the U.S. financial system.
The settlement amount reflects OFAC's assessment of the severity of the violations, as well as any mitigating or aggravating factors present in the case.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles Iran Sanctions Violations for $60,764
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its potential civil liability for eight apparent violations of U.S. sanctions on Iran, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on August 12, 2026. The violations involved its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., which exported weighing equipment to Iran through a distributor in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

The apparent violations occurred between June 2019 and November 2021, after the U.S. withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) and OFAC revoked General License H, which had previously authorized certain Iran-related transactions by foreign entities owned or controlled by U.S. persons. Despite Rice Lake's notification to Dini about the prohibition, the communication was insufficient, and Dini continued indirect sales to an Iranian end-user, Pandtec, through a UAE distributor.

OFAC determined that the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed by Rice Lake. The company launched an investigation, directed Dini to cease sales to the UAE distributor, and implemented remedial measures after receiving a tip about its products being sold in Iran.

body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on June 1, 2026. The specific details of the violations were not immediately available in the public summary.

This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions programs across various professional services sectors. Companies, including consulting firms, are expected to implement robust compliance measures to prevent engaging in prohibited transactions.
The settlement amount reflects OFAC's assessment of the violations, taking into account factors such as the nature of the conduct, the company's cooperation, and any remedial actions undertaken.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Settles with OFAC for $275,000,000
body: Adani Enterprises Limited has agreed to pay a substantial civil penalty of $275,000,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on May 18, 2026. This significant settlement underscores the severe consequences of non-compliance with U.S. sanctions laws.

The details of the apparent violations leading to this substantial penalty were not immediately disclosed in the public announcement. However, such large settlements typically involve complex and extensive breaches of sanctions regulations, often with a significant nexus to prohibited jurisdictions or activities.

This enforcement action serves as a strong reminder to multinational corporations of the critical importance of comprehensive and effective sanctions compliance programs to mitigate risks associated with global operations.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Pays $1,110,661 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on March 17, 2026. The specific nature of the violations was not immediately detailed in the public release.

This enforcement action highlights the responsibility of financial institutions, including brokerage firms, to implement robust sanctions screening and compliance measures. Failures in these areas can lead to significant penalties and reputational damage.

OFAC's actions aim to ensure that financial institutions effectively prevent sanctioned individuals and entities from accessing the U.S. financial system, thereby upholding the integrity of U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $3,777,000 Over Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on February 25, 2026. The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021.

This enforcement action underscores that U.S. sanctions laws apply to U.S. persons globally, regardless of their physical location. Individuals are expected to comply with all applicable sanctions regulations, and failures can result in substantial penalties.
OFAC's settlement with the individual reflects the agency's commitment to enforcing sanctions against those who engage in prohibited transactions with sanctioned jurisdictions, such as Syria.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Pays $1,720,000 for Kingpin Act Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a U.S.-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle apparent violations of the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on February 12, 2026. The violations involved entering into tuition enrollment agreements and processing payments for individuals designated under the Kingpin Act due to their ties to a sanctioned Mexican drug cartel.

Over a five-year period, IMG Academy processed 89 related financial transactions, including wire transfers and credit card payments, for the benefit of the designees' children. OFAC found that routine due diligence, such as screening contracting parties or payors, would have revealed that the individuals' names matched entries on the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

While the violations were deemed non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, IMG Academy's prompt and substantial cooperation, along with the implementation of a formal sanctions compliance program, were considered mitigating factors. This case highlights that academic institutions with international student bodies and foreign payors face significant sanctions exposure and must adopt risk-based controls.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes New Export Controls on Advanced AI Chips and Remote Access to Data Centers
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published an interim final rule (IFR) on November 19, 2026, imposing new export controls on advanced computing items and restricting remote access to advanced AI semiconductors. The rule targets data centers that provide significant compute power to companies headquartered in China and other countries subject to a U.S. arms embargo (Country Group D:5), as well as Macau.

This IFR formally rescinds the AI Diffusion Rule and introduces a new end-use-based license requirement for advanced computing items destined for non-U.S. data centers that provide remote access to a 'significant volume of compute power' to end users in these restricted locations. It also imposes new destination-based license requirements for exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of advanced computing items to five additional countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, citing a high risk of diversion to China.

The new rule, effective immediately upon publication, aims to prevent the circumvention of existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology through remote computing arrangements. It clarifies that providing remote access to these items is now treated as a restricted end use, even if the underlying software and commodities are never physically re-transferred to these firms. Data center operators have 90 days to obtain a BIS license for existing arrangements.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Federal Register

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
